item.title: What are AI Benchmarks?
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Wong
item.description:
In September 2026 OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra with a table of benchmark results, including 96.0% on GPQA Diamond, 97.6% on FrontierMath Tier 4 (v2), and “74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1”. Around the same time Anthropic released Fable 5.1, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, each with its own table. Each launch reports higher scores than the one before. The scores keep climbing, and it all looks impressive. But what is actually being tested? Who wrote the test, who graded it, and what does 74.1% mean?

This post opens up the benchmarks behind those tables. We treat a benchmark the way we would treat any measurement in an experiment: a sample of tasks, a procedure, a grader and an average. Seen this way, a benchmark score is an average with a standard error, just like a metric in an AB test, and it has the same kinds of biases. We start by decoding one score, “74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1”. Then we tour the benchmarks that recur in launch tables, who made them, and who grades them. Finally we look at when a high score should raise our confidence, and when we should still have doubts.

The numbers in this post are as reported by the model developers and benchmark maintainers as of October 13, 2026, unless noted otherwise.

A benchmark is an exam with three parts

Every benchmark has three parts.

  1. The tasks. A fixed set of questions or jobs, written by someone, with a known correct outcome.
  2. The harness. The program that hands each task to the model, gives the model its tools (a terminal, a browser, a code editor), and decides how long it may work and how many tries it gets.
  3. The grader. The rule that turns the model’s output into pass or fail, or into a partial score.

The headline number is the average grade over the tasks. One more question sits on top of these three parts: who ran the exam? It might be the model’s developer, the benchmark’s maintainer, or an independent evaluation organization.

A score changes when any of these parts changes. “74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1” only means something once we know all of them.

What does “74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1” mean?

DeepSWE was built by Datacurve, a company that supplies expert-written coding data, training environments and benchmarks to AI developers.

The tasks. DeepSWE has 113 tasks drawn from 91 open-source repositories, each with at least 500 GitHub stars. The repositories are written in TypeScript, Go, Python, JavaScript and Rust. Software engineers wrote each task from scratch. They came up with the problem, built the environment, wrote and verified the tests, and reviewed each other’s work. A typical task reads like a feature request. One example is adding cancellation support to Boa, a JavaScript engine written in Rust. The reference solutions are large: on average 668 added lines across 7 files.

The harness. The model works as an agent: it gets a copy of the repository and a terminal, and it can read files, run commands and edit code over many steps. For the public leaderboard, Datacurve runs every model in the same simple harness, mini-swe-agent, so that differences come from the model and not from tooling. The model finishes by committing its changes.

The grader. In version 1.1, a fresh container that the agent never touched applies the model’s changes and runs a hidden test suite. The suite contains new tests that check the requested behavior through public interfaces, plus the repository’s existing tests, which check that nothing else broke. No human and no AI reads the code to grade it. The tests do the grading. This setup is what distinguishes version 1.1 from 1.0, which uses the same tasks. Datacurve designed it to make the grader harder to game: an agent cannot patch the test framework inside the grading container, and a test that is dropped or cut short by an early exit shows up as missing or failed rather than passing.

The score. Each task is attempted many times. Datacurve notes that 73 of Claude Fable 5’s 2,260 attempts did not finish, and 2,260 / 113 = 20, so each model gets 20 attempts per task. Datacurve reports pass@1, the probability that a single attempt passes. With 20 attempts per task, a natural estimate takes the share of each task’s attempts whose code passes the hidden tests, then averages that share over all 113 tasks.

So “74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1” means: if we give GPT-6 Astra one of these 113 feature requests, its code passes the hidden tests 74.1% of the time on average, the equivalent of about 84 of the 113 tasks.

Who ran it? The 74.1% is OpenAI’s own run. Datacurve also runs Astra on its public leaderboard, in mini-swe-agent at the “xhigh” effort setting, and gets 74% ± 3%. Here the two agree. But a developer’s own run and a run by the benchmark maintainer are different measurements, and they do not always agree.

A tour of the recurring benchmarks

Some benchmarks appear in launch after launch, in four broad families. Table 1 summarizes them, and the subsections explain each one.

Software engineering: can it do a ticket?

Coding benchmarks used to be short puzzles: write a function, pass a few unit tests. Today’s coding benchmarks are agentic. The model gets a whole environment and a vague goal, much like a ticket handed to an engineer.

  • DeepSWE is described above. On Datacurve’s leaderboard, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 3.8 Flash and Claude Opus 5 are tied at the top at 74%.
  • Terminal-Bench 4.0 has 66 tasks spanning software, machine learning, science, operations, security, hardware and media. Each task runs in a real terminal, and the grader checks the final state of the machine. The project was started by Stanford and the Laude Institute in 2025. The task set is revised as models catch up: version 4.0 removed 8 tasks from 3.0 and fixed 19 others. Small models still lag far behind here. Anthropic reports Haiku 5.5 at 39.2% against Sonnet 5.5 at 70.6%.

Science and math: does it know what an expert knows?

  • GPQA (“Graduate-level Google-Proof Q&A”) was written by Rein et al. (2023). Domain experts with or pursuing PhDs wrote multiple-choice questions in biology, physics and chemistry. Other experts answered them correctly 65% of the time. Skilled non-experts managed only 34%, despite spending over 30 minutes per question with unrestricted web access. The Diamond subset keeps 198 questions on which the expert validators agreed with the answer key and most non-experts did not. Random guessing among four choices scores 25%. In 2023, the strongest GPT-4-based baseline scored 39%. OpenAI now reports 96.0% for GPT-6 Astra.
  • Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE), released by the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI in January 2025, has 2,500 questions crowdsourced from experts. About 41% are math, and the rest cover physics, biology, chemistry, computer science, the humanities and more. A question was accepted only if the frontier models of the time failed it, and only after two rounds of expert review. So by construction, the models of early 2025 scored low on it. About three quarters of the answers are short exact answers rather than multiple choice. Anthropic reports Fable 5.1 at 60.9% without tools and 65.0% with tools.
  • FrontierMath, built by Epoch AI, contains unpublished research-level math problems. Each answer is a number or a mathematical object that a program can check. Tier 4 is the hardest tier. OpenAI reports 97.6% for GPT-6 Astra on Tier 4 (v2).

Computer use and knowledge work: can it do the job?

  • OSWorld puts the model in front of a real Ubuntu desktop and asks it to do things like edit a spreadsheet in LibreOffice or change a setting in VS Code. The model sees screenshots and acts with the mouse and keyboard. The original release had 369 tasks, and the 2026 tables use the revised 2.x versions. A script then inspects the computer, for example the file contents or the config, to check that the job was done.
  • GDPval is a set of 1,320 tasks OpenAI developed in 2025 with industry professionals, spanning 44 occupations in 9 industries: write a memo, build a spreadsheet model, design a slide deck. GDPval-AA is the version run by Artificial Analysis, an independent evaluation company, on 220 of these tasks. The model works as an agent with a shell and web browsing and produces a real deliverable. Unlike everything else in the table, the score is an Elo rating, not a percentage. An AI judge sees two models’ deliverables for the same task, without names, and picks the better one. In version 2.1 the scale is anchored by fixing one reference model, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, at 1600. Only differences in Elo carry meaning: a larger gap means a higher expected win rate when two models’ deliverables are compared. Anthropic’s report of Haiku 5.5 at 1620 against Haiku 4.5 at 735 on version 2.1 means the newer model would be expected to win most head-to-head comparisons, not that it gets 1620 of anything right.

Cybersecurity: can it defend or attack?

  • CWE-bench v1, from Collinear AI, has 120 audit-and-patch tasks covering 73 categories of software weakness (CWEs) in 8 languages. The vulnerabilities are undisclosed, and the agent must find and fix them without breaking existing functionality. This is defensive work.
  • ExploitBench, from Lee and Brumley at Carnegie Mellon, is offensive. It contains 41 real bugs in V8, the JavaScript engine inside Chrome. Instead of a single pass or fail, it scores a ladder of 16 capabilities: from triggering the bug, through gaining read and write access to memory, up to arbitrary code execution. A deterministic verifier checks each rung. The exploit must work against the buggy version and fail against the patched one.

Who grades the AI?

Across Table 1 there are three kinds of graders, and they deserve different levels of trust.

  1. Programs. Hidden tests (DeepSWE, CWE-bench), check scripts on the final state of a machine (Terminal-Bench, OSWorld), answer keys (GPQA, FrontierMath) and exploit verifiers (ExploitBench). These graders are mechanical and reproducible. Their weakness is that a test can only check what its author thought to check.
  2. AI judges. HLE uses an AI model (o3-mini in the original paper) to decide whether an answer like “0.5” matches a key that says “1/2”. GDPval-AA uses an AI judge to compare deliverables, because no test can check whether a memo is persuasive. Datacurve also used an AI model to audit DeepSWE’s own tests. When the grader is itself a model, the score inherits the grader’s blind spots and tastes.
  3. Humans. Humans rarely grade the model directly, because human grading is slow and expensive. They show up earlier: they write the tasks and answer keys (DeepSWE’s engineers, GDPval’s professionals), and they validate the questions (GPQA’s expert and non-expert validators, HLE’s expert reviewers).

Who runs the exam?

A benchmark is not a sealed exam administered by a testing agency. Most are published openly: the tasks, the grader and often a reference harness are available for anyone to download and run against any model they can access. DeepSWE’s repository contains all 113 tasks with their tests and grader configuration, plus a quickstart that runs the benchmark with Datacurve’s Pier tool. The mini-swe-agent harness that Datacurve uses for its leaderboard is also open source, as is Terminal-Bench. The questions for GPQA and HLE are on Hugging Face; GPQA is gated, so we must request access and accept its terms first. Evaluation frameworks package many benchmarks with a ready-made harness and grader. The UK AI Security Institute’s Inspect Evals includes GPQA, HLE and OSWorld, and EleutherAI’s lm-evaluation-harness covers a wide range of question-and-answer benchmarks.

The model is the other half. Frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 cannot be downloaded: we reach them through their developers’ APIs with an API key, and the harness sends each task to the API. Open-weight models can be downloaded from Hugging Face, for example OpenAI’s gpt-oss-20b, and run on our own hardware. Either way, the same benchmark can be run by several different groups, and a score is only as informative as our knowledge of who ran it and how. Three groups do most of the running.

  1. The model’s developer, in house. Most numbers in a launch table come from the developer’s own evaluation team, running the benchmark on its own infrastructure before release. OpenAI’s launch post says its GPT evaluations “were run in our research environment or via our API”, which “may provide slightly different output from production ChatGPT due to differences in the system prompts, tools available, etc.” The developer chooses the harness and the settings, and OpenAI reports the maximum score at any effort setting. For competitors’ columns, a developer either copies the competitor’s published number, which OpenAI’s charts label “reported score only”, or runs the competitor’s model itself through that competitor’s public API. OpenAI did the latter for HealthBench Professional: “we independently evaluated all Claude models following the intended HealthBench Professional procedure.”
  2. The benchmark’s maintainer. Some maintainers run models themselves and publish a leaderboard. Datacurve runs every model on DeepSWE in the same harness, mini-swe-agent, so that differences come from the models rather than the tooling. This is how we got Datacurve’s 74% ± 3% for Astra, next to OpenAI’s in-house 74.1%. Maintainers sometimes test a model before its launch: OpenAI’s post quotes the ARC Prize Foundation, which maintains ARC-AGI-3, on its own testing of Astra, calling it “the best model we’ve ever tested”.
  3. Independent evaluation organizations. Companies like Artificial Analysis run many benchmarks across many models in one shared setup, and publish the results. They run GDPval-AA, and combined indices such as the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, which OpenAI’s own table reports. They usually test models through the same public API that customers use, and sometimes get access before launch: Anthropic’s Sonnet 5.5 page notes that Artificial Analysis tested a pre-release deployment.

A launch table usually mixes all three, and the footnotes often say which is which. The in-house runs are the most numerous and come with the developer’s choices of harness and settings. The maintainer and independent runs are fewer, but they apply one setup to every model. When an in-house number and an independent number for the same model agree, as Astra’s do on DeepSWE, we learn that the result does not hinge on who ran it.

When a high score should raise our confidence

A high score is real evidence when the measurement was designed well. These are the properties to look for.

  1. The tasks are new to the model. DeepSWE’s tasks were written from scratch rather than adapted from public commits, so they were not on the internet before the benchmark was released. HLE keeps a private set of questions that is never published. A benchmark built from material that appeared after the model’s knowledge cutoff is the strongest version of this.
  2. The grader checks the outcome, and the grader itself was audited. Datacurve used an AI reviewer to audit the tests of DeepSWE v1.0 on a sample of 30 tasks. They found a 0.3% false-positive rate (passing a bad patch) and a 1.1% false-negative rate (failing a good one). The same check on SWE-Bench Pro, an earlier and widely used coding benchmark, gave 8.5% and 24%. An audit applies to the version it checked.
  3. Someone else reproduced it. OpenAI’s 74.1% for Astra on DeepSWE agrees with Datacurve’s independent 74% ± 3%. When the developer’s number and the maintainer’s number agree, the result does not depend on who ran it.
  4. Many benchmarks agree. One benchmark can have a quirk. A model that leads in coding, science and computer use at once is unlikely to owe all of it to quirks.
  5. The tasks resemble the consumer’s task. By the consumer we mean the team that will use the model for its own work. A consumer writing Go services learns more from DeepSWE than from GPQA, and a consumer automating spreadsheets learns more from OSWorld.
  6. The gap is bigger than the noise. A score is an average over a sample of tasks, so it has a standard error. For a sense of its size, suppose each of tasks were attempted once, and the model passes each one independently with probability . Then the score is a sample proportion, with standard error . For DeepSWE, plugging in and gives , about 4 points. Datacurve’s leaderboard prints error bars of ±1 to ±6 points, the same range. As with the minimum detectable effect in an AB test, a lead of a few points on about a hundred tasks may just be noise, which we describe next.

How much noise is in a benchmark score?

Datacurve’s leaderboard puts GPT-6 Astra at 74% on DeepSWE and Claude Fable 5 at 70%, both run by Datacurve in the same harness. Is a 4-point lead a real difference in skill, or the luck of which 113 tasks happened to be on the exam? In point 6 of the previous section we sized the noise as if each task were attempted once, and got about 4 points. DeepSWE attempts each task 20 times, so we need a closer look.

We can think of DeepSWE’s 113 tasks as a sample from a much larger population of feature requests that could have been written. Each task has a probability , a scalar between 0 and 1, that the model solves it on a single attempt. The quantity we actually care about is the model’s skill on the whole population, , where the expectation averages over the population of tasks. This is the same as in point 6, now allowed to differ from task to task. Datacurve’s per-task results show that pass rates vary widely across tasks, and that a task one model solves every time can be one another model rarely solves.

The benchmark score is a sample estimate of . With tasks and attempts per task, let be the fraction of the attempts on task that pass. The score is

varies for two reasons. The attempts are random, so rerunning the same tasks gives slightly different . And the tasks are random: the benchmark’s 113 tasks are one draw from the population, and a different 113 feature requests would give a different average.

To see how large each source is, we simulate a world that looks like DeepSWE. We build a pool of 10,000 possible tasks, each with a difficulty, and two models A and B with exactly the same average skill on the pool. The models are not identical task by task. Each has its own strengths, so and are correlated but not equal. Real models share many of the same hard tasks, but not all of them.

Code 
set.seed(2026)

N_pool <- 10000  # possible tasks that could have been written
n <- 113         # tasks on the benchmark
K <- 20          # attempts per task

# Each task has a difficulty d_j. Each model's solve probability on task j
# depends on the difficulty plus a model-specific strength or weakness on that task.
pool <- tibble(j = 1:N_pool, d_j = rnorm(N_pool, 0, 1.5)) |>
  mutate(
    theta_A = plogis(1.6 - d_j + rnorm(N_pool, 0, 1)),
    theta_B = plogis(1.6 - d_j + rnorm(N_pool, 0, 1))
  )

pool |>
  summarise(
    p_A = mean(theta_A),
    p_B = mean(theta_B),
    cor_theta_A_B = cor(theta_A, theta_B),
    theta_A_10pct = quantile(theta_A, 0.1),
    theta_A_90pct = quantile(theta_A, 0.9)
  )
# A tibble: 1 × 5
    p_A   p_B cor_theta_A_B theta_A_10pct theta_A_90pct
  <dbl> <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
1 0.742 0.740         0.651         0.332         0.980

Both models have a true skill of about 74% on the pool, close to the top of today’s leaderboard. Per-task solve rates range from about a third on hard tasks to nearly 1 on easy ones. Now we run the benchmark 2,000 times in two ways. First we keep the same 113 tasks and only redraw the attempts. Then we draw a fresh set of 113 tasks each time.

Code 
run_benchmark <- function(tasks) {
  tasks |>
    mutate(
      s_A = rbinom(n(), K, theta_A) / K,
      s_B = rbinom(n(), K, theta_B) / K
    ) |>
    summarise(p_hat_A = mean(s_A), p_hat_B = mean(s_B))
}

fixed_tasks <- slice_sample(pool, n = n)

sims <- bind_rows(
  map(1:2000, \(r) run_benchmark(fixed_tasks)) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    mutate(source = "Same 113 tasks, new attempts"),
  map(1:2000, \(r) run_benchmark(slice_sample(pool, n = n))) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    mutate(source = "New 113 tasks each time")
) |>
  mutate(gap = p_hat_A - p_hat_B)

sim_summary <- sims |>
  group_by(source) |>
  summarise(
    sd_p_hat_A = sd(p_hat_A),
    mean_gap = mean(gap),
    sd_gap = sd(gap),
    share_gap_at_least_4 = mean(abs(gap) >= 0.04)
  )
sim_summary
# A tibble: 2 × 5
  source                       sd_p_hat_A mean_gap sd_gap share_gap_at_least_4
  <chr>                             <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>                <dbl>
1 New 113 tasks each time         0.0247   0.00156 0.0227               0.0755
2 Same 113 tasks, new attempts    0.00757  0.0185  0.0107               0.024
Code 
fixed_row <- filter(sim_summary, source == "Same 113 tasks, new attempts")
fresh_row <- filter(sim_summary, source == "New 113 tasks each time")
Code 
ggplot(sims, aes(x = 100 * gap, fill = source)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-4, 4), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e")) +
  labs(x = "Score of A minus score of B (points)", y = "Simulated runs", fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

Some patterns worth noting:

  1. Rerunning the attempts barely moves the score. With the tasks held fixed, the standard deviation of a model’s score is 0.8 points. Twenty attempts per task average away most of the run-to-run randomness.
  2. With fixed tasks, the gap is centered on A’s advantage on those tasks, not on zero. On this particular set of 113 tasks, model A’s average is 1.9 points above B’s, even though the two are equally skilled on the pool. Rerunning the attempts scatters the gap around that value with a standard deviation of 1.1 points, and the gap reaches 4 points in 2% of reruns. This is not a null distribution for “A and B are equally skilled”. It is the distribution of the gap when A really is ahead on these fixed tasks, so the 2% is not a p-value. Rerunning the same exam many times would not reveal that A’s advantage comes from the choice of tasks.
  3. The choice of tasks is the main source of noise. With a fresh draw of tasks, a single model’s score has a standard deviation of 2.5 points. That is the uncertainty in the claim “this model solves 74% of feature requests like these”. It is smaller than the single-attempt figure of about 4 points from point 6, because the 20 attempts average away the coin flips within each task. It is also in the range of the ±1 to ±4 points that Datacurve prints for its top three models.
  4. The fresh-task runs are the null distribution. Here the two models are equally skilled on the population, each run draws a new set of tasks, and both models are graded on the same tasks, as on a real benchmark. So this is the null distribution for the question we care about: is A better than B on feature requests like these in general? The gap is centered near zero, with a standard deviation of 2.3 points, and it is 4 or more points in either direction in 7.5% of runs. In this world, a 4-point lead, like Astra’s over Fable 5, has a two-sided p-value of about 0.075. It is not significant at the 5% level.

The two simulations answer different questions. If we asked instead whether A is better on these exact 113 tasks, the null would be centered at zero with the fixed-task spread of 1.1 points. A 4-point gap would then be 3.7 standard deviations out, which is highly significant. But that question is narrow: with 20 attempts per task, almost any real difference on a fixed task set is detectable. A benchmark is useful because we want to generalize beyond its tasks, and that is the question with the wider null.

These numbers depend on the assumptions in our simulated world, in particular how much the models’ strengths differ task by task. They are not a statement about Astra or Fable 5. The general lesson holds: a benchmark of about a hundred tasks cannot reliably separate models a few points apart. This is the same arithmetic as the minimum detectable effect in an AB test. A small sample of tasks has a large MDE.

Testing a gap with a paired comparison

With real data we cannot simulate the null, but we can estimate its spread from a single benchmark run. For each task , let be the difference in the two models’ pass rates. The gap in scores is the average difference,

If the tasks are a random sample from the population, the are independent draws, so is a sample mean with standard error , and . Each includes both sources of noise, the task’s difficulty for each model and the randomness of the attempts, so this standard error accounts for both. Pairing matters. A hard task lowers both and , and taking the difference cancels the shared part. This is the same logic as a within-user comparison in an AB test, with tasks in the role of users.

We can test this on one simulated benchmark run, and compare the paired standard error with the spread of the gap across the 2,000 fresh benchmarks. We also compute the unpaired standard error, which treats the two scores as if they came from independent task sets.

Code 
set.seed(7)

one_run <- slice_sample(pool, n = n) |>
  mutate(
    s_A = rbinom(n(), K, theta_A) / K,
    s_B = rbinom(n(), K, theta_B) / K,
    d_j = s_A - s_B
  )

paired_test <- one_run |>
  summarise(
    d_bar = mean(d_j),
    se_paired = sd(d_j) / sqrt(n()),
    se_unpaired = sqrt(var(s_A) + var(s_B)) / sqrt(n()),
    z = d_bar / se_paired
  )
paired_test
# A tibble: 1 × 4
     d_bar se_paired se_unpaired      z
     <dbl>     <dbl>       <dbl>  <dbl>
1 -0.00619    0.0224      0.0346 -0.276

The paired standard error from this one run is 2.2 points, close to the 2.3-point spread of the gap across the fresh benchmarks. The unpaired standard error is 3.5 points. It overstates the noise, because it ignores that both models faced the same tasks. With per-task results for two real models, the same calculation would give a p-value for their gap without any simulation.

Being rigorous about what we read

Noise shrinks as a benchmark adds tasks. The problems below are different. They are biases: each one shifts the score systematically, up or down depending on the problem, and adding more tasks does not fix them.

The model may have seen the exam

Models are trained on large amounts of internet text. If benchmark questions, or their solutions, are on the internet, a model can score well by remembering rather than reasoning. This is called contamination, and it pushes scores up.

ExploitBench shows how contamination can be measured. Its 41 bugs are real V8 vulnerabilities disclosed in 2024 or later. Their descriptions, patches and bug-tracker discussions are public, although working exploits were published for only 2 of them. OpenAI reported that GPT-6 Astra reached arbitrary code execution on all 41, a score of 100%.

In the same launch post, OpenAI raised the question itself: “given concerns that exposure to historical software vulnerabilities may have affected benchmark results”, it also built an internal set of 20 high-severity V8 vulnerabilities disclosed between June and August 2026, after the model’s knowledge cutoff. Astra scored 39.0% on that set, against 5.5% for GPT-5.6 Sol. OpenAI notes that some of these vulnerabilities may not permit arbitrary code execution under the evaluation’s constraints, so 100% may not be achievable there. It also reports that Astra found two previously unknown vulnerabilities during the evaluation, which OpenAI is disclosing to their maintainers.

The two sets contain different bugs, so the scores are not directly comparable. Epoch AI’s review attributes part of the 100% to contamination, and notes that the size of the effect is hard to quantify. For newly disclosed vulnerabilities, the 39.0% is the more direct measurement, and running such a check is what makes the 100% interpretable.

Benchmark maintainers watch for this too. When Terminal-Bench moved to version 4.0, it removed 2 tasks because their solutions had become public.

Exposure can also come from how a benchmark is funded and shared. OpenAI commissioned Epoch AI to produce 300 advanced math problems for FrontierMath, owns them, and has access to the problems and their solutions. Epoch AI also maintains a separate holdout set of 50 problems, for which OpenAI receives only the problem statements, so that every lab’s models can be tested on solutions no lab has seen. When reading a FrontierMath score, it helps to know whether it was measured on the holdout set.

The answer key can be wrong

Benchmarks are written by people, and people make mistakes. When the grader is wrong, the error can push scores in either direction.

DeepSWE. Epoch AI reviews popular benchmarks. On September 7, 2026 it rated DeepSWE v1.1 “Flawed”. It found false negatives, where correct work is marked as failing, in at least 23 of the 113 tasks (20.3%). It stopped inspecting once the errors passed its published 20% threshold, so there may be more. 78% of these errors were collisions. The verifier adds its hidden tests to the model’s changes, so when the model had written its own test with the same name as a hidden one, the test package failed to compile. The models had no way to know this and were not told to avoid it. These errors push DeepSWE scores down.

Errors in the other direction have been reported too. On October 2, 2026 an outside audit firm opened a public issue on DeepSWE’s repository showing false positives. A submitted patch can change test infrastructure that the verifier then loads. In one example, a patch that only edited a test configuration file, rewriting failed test reports as passes, received full credit without implementing the feature. As of this writing the issue is open, with no public response from Datacurve.

HLE. In July 2025, FutureHouse reported that 29% ± 3.7% (95% confidence interval) of the answers to HLE’s text-only chemistry and biology questions conflicted with the peer-reviewed literature. That estimate came from 321 questions, checked by FutureHouse’s literature-search agent and validated by expert reviewers on a sample. In September 2025, FutureHouse posted an update: the HLE team’s own review, in which three experts examined each question in a subset of the biology and chemistry questions, found about 18% of them problematic. At least one of the three experts disagreed with the answer in about 25% of cases. The two estimates differ, but both are far from zero. The HLE organizers responded by committing to a rolling revision process for the benchmark.

A wrong answer key puts a ceiling on the score. If a fraction of the answer key is wrong, a model that always gives the truly correct answer is marked wrong on those questions and scores at most . The HLE team found about 18% of the questions they reviewed problematic. If all of those had wrong answers, and the ceiling on those questions would be 82%. Near the ceiling, we cannot tell a better model from one that better matches the mistakes in the key.

The harness and settings are part of the score

The same model gets different scores under different harnesses and settings. The differences can be larger than the gaps between models:

  • On ExploitBench, GPT-5.5 running in OpenAI’s Codex harness reached arbitrary code execution 12 times when allowed 3,000 turns. With a 300-turn limit, it reached it 0 times in the Codex harness and once without it. OpenAI’s launch post makes the same point about its own models: GPT-5.6 Sol’s 5.5% on the June–August set is an artifact of that set’s 300-turn limit, and Sol scored 11.5% at similar settings with fewer limits.
  • Scores are usually reported at a high “effort” or reasoning budget, which costs more and takes longer than many production settings. OpenAI’s table states that its “evaluation scores are the maximum at any effort”. Anthropic’s footnote for Opus 5.5 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 says the reported number is the model’s highest score, obtained at the “xhigh” effort setting.
  • More effort is not always better. On FrontierCode, a coding benchmark that penalizes changes outside the task’s scope, Sonnet 5.5 scored lower at its maximum effort setting than at xhigh. At maximum effort it ran additional code-review subagents, which occasionally caused timeouts or extra edits.
  • On OSWorld 2.0 tasks where Anthropic’s production safeguards intervened, Fable 5.1 scored zero. Here the deployment setup lowers the score.

The same name can mean different scores

Sonnet 5.5 appears with two different OSWorld 2.1 numbers on Anthropic’s own pages: 80.1% under a “partial” scoring rule on the Sonnet launch page, and 83.9% on an “offline subset” of the tasks on the Haiku launch page. Fable 5.1 is reported at 77.9% on OSWorld 2.0 under the “partial” rule and 41.7% under a “strict” one. Neither number is wrong, but they are different measurements.

Benchmarks also get revised. Terminal-Bench calls version 4.0 a breaking change that requires re-running trials, because it changed both the task set and the resources given to the agent. So a model’s score on 4.0 cannot be compared with an older model’s score on 3.0. Anthropic’s OSWorld 2.0 scores use the benchmark authors’ August 2026 task release, and Anthropic re-ran its older models under the same conditions. That is the right practice, and it is worth checking for whenever a table compares models across versions.

The benchmark does not represent the consumer’s task

Even a perfect benchmark measures the model on its own task distribution. It’s not necessarily what the consumer cares most about. DeepSWE’s tasks are in five languages, from open-source repositories with at least 500 GitHub stars, each with a written task description. The consumer’s codebase may be private, old, underspecified and in a language the benchmark does not cover. A benchmark tells the consumer which models are worth trying. Whether a model improves the consumer’s product is still a causal question about that product’s users, and the final judge is an AB test.

Putting it together

When we read the next launch table, these questions help us interpret each row.

Question Why it matters Example
What are the tasks, and who wrote them? Defines what the score measures DeepSWE: 113 feature requests written from scratch
Could the model have seen them? Contamination inflates scores ExploitBench: 100% on public bugs, 39.0% on a newer, different set
Who or what grades the output? Tests, scripts, AI judges and humans fail differently HLE and GDPval-AA both use AI judges
Has the answer key been audited? Grading errors can lower, inflate or cap the score Epoch found errors in at least 20% of DeepSWE tasks
Who ran it, and with what harness and settings? Settings can move scores by more than the gaps between models ExploitBench: 300 vs 3,000 turns
Which version and scoring rule? Same name, different measurement OSWorld 2.0 partial 77.9% vs strict 41.7%
Is the gap bigger than the noise? About 100 tasks give a standard error of a few points DeepSWE: about 4 points at 74% on 113 tasks; the top three models are tied at 74%
Do the tasks look like the consumer’s task? A benchmark measures its own task distribution The consumer still needs its own AB test

A benchmark score is a measurement, not a verdict. It’s an average over a sample of tasks, produced by a harness and a grader that someone chose, and often run by the model’s developer. High scores across fresh, audited, independently reproduced benchmarks are strong evidence that a model has improved. A lead of a few points on a single benchmark is weaker evidence, whoever ran it. The scores will keep going up. Each time, it’s worth asking what the exam was.

item.title: First Principles of Ranking
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Wong
item.description:
It is Friday night, and a member opens Netflix on their TV. Within a second, the home page fills with rows of titles: “Continue Watching”, “Trending Now”, “Because You Watched Titanic”, “Top Picks for You”. Behind every one of those rows is a ranker. A ranker receives a query, here the member and their context, picks a handful of titles out of a catalog of thousands, and decides what order to show them in.

The stakes are high and the time is short. Netflix reports that a typical member loses interest after perhaps 60 to 90 seconds of choosing, having reviewed 10 to 20 titles on one or two screens, and that recommendations influence about 80% of the hours streamed (Gomez-Uribe and Hunt, 2015). If the right title is not in the first few tiles of the first few rows, the member may never find it.

This post builds a ranker from first principles, using a single Netflix row, “Top Picks for You”, as the running example. We will start from the problem we would like to solve, see why it is intractable, and watch the standard three phase architecture fall out of the approximations we are forced to make:

  1. Candidate generation: cheaply narrow the whole catalog down to a few hundred titles.
  2. Utility prediction: use an expensive ML model to predict how much the member will value each candidate.
  3. Reranking: assemble the final row, accounting for the fact that titles in a row interact with one another.

Netflix has described parts of its system publicly, and we cite those descriptions where they exist. Elsewhere, the Netflix setting is our illustration of how a method would apply, not a claim about what Netflix runs in production.

The problem we would like to solve

Let the catalog contain items, indexed by . In our example, an item is a title, and is in the thousands. A query arrives. On the home page, is the member and their context: their viewing history, the device (a TV, not a phone), and the time (Friday night). When the member types into the search box, also includes the text. We must display a row of titles in order,

where is the title shown at position . Let be the utility generated by showing row to query : the probability that the member presses play, the expected minutes they stream, or whatever we value. The ideal ranker solves

There are ordered rows. With titles and tiles, that is roughly rows. We cannot evaluate them all, so we need structure.

The naive solution

The simplest structure comes from a model of how members scan a row. Say the member examines position with probability , where . On a TV, only the first few tiles of a row are visible before the member scrolls right, and the 60 to 90 second attention span means most never scroll far. If the member examines title , it generates expected utility , a scalar. Make two assumptions:

  • (A1) No interactions. The utility of title does not depend on which other titles are in the row.
  • (A2) Exhaustive scoring. We can evaluate for every one of the titles.

Under (A1), the row utility is a weighted sum over positions,

The optimal row sorts the titles by .

The three phases of a ranker exist because these assumptions fail in different ways.

  • (A2) fails because a good model of is expensive, and it must run for every row on every home page that every member opens. Candidate generation exists to cut down to a manageable .
  • is unknown. Utility prediction estimates it with an ML model, .
  • (A1) fails because titles in a row do interact: a row of ten romantic comedies is worth less than ten times one romantic comedy, because the member only needs one of them. Reranking exists to optimize the row as a whole.

Phase 1: Candidate generation

The job of candidate generation is to return a set of titles, where . For the “Top Picks” row, think of a few hundred candidates out of 10,000 titles. The scoring here must be cheap, much cheaper than the model in phase 2, so it will be less accurate. Netflix’s catalog is small compared with services that rank hundreds of millions of videos or products, so its funnel can be shallower, but the logic is the same.

Candidate generation is a ceiling on the entire system. If a title is not retrieved, no downstream model can ever show it. So candidate generation is judged by recall, not precision. Let be the set of the titles with the highest true utility. Then

The numerator counts how many titles of the ideal row survived retrieval, and dividing by turns that count into the fraction of the ideal row that is still within reach of phases 2 and 3. Equivalently, it is the probability that a title drawn at random from the ideal row made it into the candidate set. Even if the downstream phases were perfect, the best row they could build would contain only of the ideal titles. Note that the denominator is , not : retrieving extra titles that are not in the ideal row costs nothing in this metric, which is why candidate generators are free to return far more titles than the row can show.

How large does need to be? Suppose the cheap scorer produces a score that is correlated with the true utility (dropping for now) with correlation ,

For each of 200 members, we retrieve the top titles by out of , and ask what fraction of that member’s true top we caught.

Code 
set.seed(1)
N <- 1e4          # titles in the catalog
K <- 20           # tiles in the row
n_members <- 200
M_grid <- round(10^seq(log10(K), log10(N), length.out = 25))

# Recall@M at every candidate set size M, for one simulated member
recall_curve <- function(rho) {
  u <- rnorm(N)
  eps <- rnorm(N)
  s <- rho * u + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * eps
  top_K <- order(u, decreasing = TRUE)[1:K]
  ord <- order(s, decreasing = TRUE)
  tibble(M = M_grid, recall = map_dbl(M_grid, \(M) mean(top_K %in% ord[1:M])))
}

recall <- expand_grid(rho = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.95), member = 1:n_members) %>%
  mutate(curve = map(rho, recall_curve)) %>%
  unnest(curve) %>%
  group_by(rho, M) %>%
  summarise(recall = mean(recall), .groups = "drop")

With a correlation of 0.8, a candidate set of about 200 titles, ten times the row, recovers only about three quarters of the true top 20, and it takes more than 400 titles to recover 90%. This is why candidate generation returns hundreds of titles rather than exactly , and why it pays to combine several cheap scorers that make different mistakes. Below are the most common ones.

Lexical retrieval

When the member types into the search box, the oldest method is to match words. Lexical retrieval needs no training data, and it handles exact matches on rare terms, such as an actor’s name, which embedding models can blur. An inverted index maps each term to the list of titles whose text (name, synopsis, cast) contains it. When the member searches for “heist”, we look up the entry for “heist” and get back only the titles whose text mentions a heist, rather than scanning all titles. Matched titles are scored with a formula such as BM25,

Here is the term frequency, the number of times term appears in title ’s text, is the length of that text, is the average length, and are tuning constants (usually written and ; we rename them to avoid a clash with position ). is the inverse document frequency, which grows as fewer titles contain , for example where is the number of titles containing . Each piece has a job:

  • says rare words are more informative than common ones. Nearly every synopsis contains “the”, but few contain “heist”.
  • The fraction saturates as grows: it is bounded by . A synopsis that says “heist” five times is not five times more relevant than one that says it once.
  • The term discounts long texts, such as a documentary series with a long episode guide, which contain many terms by chance.

On the BEIR benchmark, which evaluates retrievers on domains they were not trained on, BM25 proved to be a robust baseline that many neural retrievers failed to beat (Thakur et al., 2021).

The weakness of lexical retrieval is vocabulary mismatch. A member who types “bank robbery movies” does not match a synopsis that only says “a crew of thieves plans the perfect heist”.

Collaborative filtering

The “Top Picks” row has no search text at all, so we need to use behavior. Netflix made this problem famous with the Netflix Prize. In 2006, Netflix released about 100 million movie ratings and offered $1 million to anyone who could improve the root mean squared error of its in-house rating predictor, Cinematch, by 10%. The data contained no movie descriptions to speak of, only who rated what. Here, the query is simply the member, with no other context, and an item is a movie. The question is which movies a member will like, based only on the viewing history of that member and of everyone else.

The simplest approach is item-to-item collaborative filtering, which Amazon described in Linden, Smith and York (2003). If many members who watched movie also watched movie , then is a good candidate for anyone who just watched . To make this precise, arrange engagement into a matrix with one row per member and one column per movie, where records member ’s engagement with movie , for example if member watched movie and 0 otherwise. Column of , written , lists every member’s engagement with movie .

Consider a tiny Netflix with seven members and six movies: three romances (Notebook, Titanic, La La Land) and three action movies (Die Hard, The Matrix, Alien). We will come back to these movies throughout the post.

Code 
Y <- rbind(
  c(1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0),
  c(1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0),
  c(0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0),
  c(0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0),
  c(0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1),
  c(0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1),
  c(1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)
)
dimnames(Y) <- list(paste0("member", 1:7),
                    c("Notebook", "Titanic", "LaLaLand", "DieHard", "Matrix", "Alien"))
Y
        Notebook Titanic LaLaLand DieHard Matrix Alien
member1        1       1        0       0      0     0
member2        1       0        1       0      0     0
member3        0       1        1       1      0     0
member4        0       0        0       1      1     0
member5        0       0        1       0      1     1
member6        0       0        0       1      0     1
member7        1       1        1       0      0     0

The item-by-item co-occurrence matrix is , whose entries are inner products of columns,

With 0/1 engagement, counts the members who watched both and , and the diagonal entry counts the members who watched at all. Raw counts favor popular movies, since a blockbuster co-occurs with almost everything, so the counts are normalized. Dividing by the lengths of the two columns gives the cosine similarity between them,

Movie ’s neighbor list is the handful of movies with the largest , stored with their scores. The name comes from nearest neighbors: if we think of movies as points and similarity as closeness, the list holds movie ’s nearest neighbors. In our tiny Netflix, Notebook was watched by members 1, 2 and 7. Titanic was watched by members 1, 3 and 7, an overlap of two members, so . La La Land was watched by members 2, 3, 5 and 7, also an overlap of two, so . No one who watched Notebook watched an action movie. Notebook’s neighbor list is (Titanic 0.67, La La Land 0.58). We can compute every movie’s similarities at once.

Code 
YtY <- t(Y) %*% Y                            # co-occurrence counts
sim <- YtY / sqrt(diag(YtY) %o% diag(YtY))   # cosine similarity between columns of Y
round(sim, 2)
         Notebook Titanic LaLaLand DieHard Matrix Alien
Notebook     1.00    0.67     0.58    0.00   0.00  0.00
Titanic      0.67    1.00     0.58    0.33   0.00  0.00
LaLaLand     0.58    0.58     1.00    0.29   0.35  0.35
DieHard      0.00    0.33     0.29    1.00   0.41  0.41
Matrix       0.00    0.00     0.35    0.41   1.00  0.50
Alien        0.00    0.00     0.35    0.41   0.50  1.00

The neighbor lists are computed offline into a lookup table. At request time, we look up the lists of the member’s recent movies, take their union, and score each candidate by the sum of its similarities to the member’s movies. No model runs at request time, which is why this method is very cheap. This is exactly the shape of Netflix’s “Because You Watched” row, which Gomez-Uribe and Hunt describe as driven by an unpersonalized “sims” algorithm that computes a ranked list of similar videos for every video in the catalog.

Matrix factorization

The approach that dominated the Netflix Prize was matrix factorization. Early in the competition, Simon Funk described a simple version in a blog post, Try This at Home, that jumped near the top of the leaderboard. The winning teams built on it, as summarized by Koren, Bell and Volinsky (2009). Netflix later wrote that it put a matrix factorization model (SVD), together with a restricted Boltzmann machine, into production after the competition.

Return to the engagement matrix . Rather than comparing its columns pairwise, we approximate the whole matrix. Any real matrix has a singular value decomposition (SVD)

where is the rank of , has one row per member and orthonormal columns, has one row per movie ( rows) and orthonormal columns, and is an diagonal matrix of singular values sorted so that . Keep only the first columns of and and the first singular values, written , and . Then

is a rank matrix, and by the Eckart–Young theorem it is the closest rank matrix to in the sum of squared entries. To get two embedding matrices, split evenly between the two sides,

each with columns. Row of is member ’s embedding, and row of is movie ’s embedding. Write them as column vectors . Since , the two matrices multiply back to the rank approximation,

So the predicted affinity of member for movie is entry of , which is a dot product of the two embeddings,

Each of the dimensions acts like a latent taste. measures how much movie expresses taste , measures how much member has it, and measures how much of the variation in that taste explains. The recommendations come from what the approximation gets “wrong”. A rank matrix cannot reproduce every 0 in , so a movie the member has not watched, but that resembles the movies they did watch, gets a positive . Those are the candidates. The split of is a convention; and give the same .

Let’s factor the tiny Netflix matrix from above.

Code 
d <- 2
svd_Y <- svd(Y)
# The signs of singular vectors are arbitrary; flip them so that Notebook loads positively on each dimension
flip <- sign(svd_Y$v[1, 1:d])
W_d <- svd_Y$u[, 1:d] %*% diag(flip)
V_d <- svd_Y$v[, 1:d] %*% diag(flip)
Sigma_d <- diag(svd_Y$d[1:d])

Phi <- W_d %*% sqrt(Sigma_d)
Psi <- V_d %*% sqrt(Sigma_d)
dimnames(Phi) <- list(rownames(Y), c("taste1", "taste2"))
dimnames(Psi) <- list(colnames(Y), c("taste1", "taste2"))
round(Psi, 2)
         taste1 taste2
Notebook   0.75   0.64
Titanic    0.83   0.40
LaLaLand   1.07  -0.02
DieHard    0.50  -0.78
Matrix     0.31  -0.66
Alien      0.31  -0.66

The first dimension is positive for every movie. It measures how much a movie is watched overall. The second dimension separates Notebook and Titanic (positive) from the action movies (negative), which the SVD discovered without being told any genres. La La Land sits near zero because fans of both genres watched it. Multiplying the embeddings gives the predicted affinities.

Code 
Y_hat <- Phi %*% t(Psi)
round(Y_hat, 2)
        Notebook Titanic LaLaLand DieHard Matrix Alien
member1     0.75    0.67     0.59   -0.12  -0.16 -0.16
member2     0.68    0.65     0.68    0.08   0.00  0.00
member3     0.51    0.62     0.90    0.57   0.39  0.39
member4    -0.23   -0.04     0.32    0.69   0.55  0.55
member5     0.03    0.23     0.65    0.80   0.62  0.62
member6    -0.23   -0.04     0.32    0.69   0.55  0.55
member7     1.03    0.97     0.99    0.08  -0.04 -0.04

Look at member 3, who watched Titanic, La La Land and Die Hard. Among the movies they have not watched, Notebook scores 0.51 and The Matrix and Alien score 0.39, so the top candidate is the romance, in line with two of their three movies. Member 4 watched Die Hard and The Matrix. Their top unwatched movie is Alien at 0.55, the remaining action movie.

Missing is not the same as zero

The SVD needs every entry of . For watch data, a 0 meaning “did not watch” is reasonable. For the star ratings in the Netflix Prize it is not: a missing rating does not mean the member would rate the movie 0 stars. It means we do not know.

To see this, give our tiny Netflix star ratings. Let be the matrix of ratings, with the same rows and columns as , where is member ’s rating of movie , and let be the set of pairs for which a rating exists. Each member has rated four of the six movies, including some movies they disliked, and the other two ratings are missing.

Code 
Y_star <- rbind(
  c( 5,  4, NA,  1, NA,  2),
  c( 4, NA,  5,  2,  1, NA),
  c(NA,  5,  4,  2, NA,  1),
  c( 1, NA,  2,  5,  4, NA),
  c(NA,  1,  2, NA,  5,  4),
  c( 2,  1, NA,  4, NA,  5),
  c( 5,  5,  4, NA,  2, NA)
)
dimnames(Y_star) <- dimnames(Y)
Y_star
        Notebook Titanic LaLaLand DieHard Matrix Alien
member1        5       4       NA       1     NA     2
member2        4      NA        5       2      1    NA
member3       NA       5        4       2     NA     1
member4        1      NA        2       5      4    NA
member5       NA       1        2      NA      5     4
member6        2       1       NA       4     NA     5
member7        5       5        4      NA      2    NA

Members 1, 2, 3 and 7 like the romances and members 4, 5 and 6 like the action movies, but each member is missing two ratings. Filling the missing entries with 0 would tell the SVD that member 1 rated La La Land lower than Die Hard, which they gave 1 star.

Fitting only the observed ratings

Funk’s method, despite being called SVD, does not compute a decomposition at all. It never fills in the missing entries. Instead, it chooses the embeddings to fit only the observed ratings, with a ridge penalty to avoid overfitting,

Here is a scalar, the average of the observed ratings. Subtracting it means the embeddings only have to explain how a rating differs from a typical rating, and the ridge penalty shrinks predictions toward rather than toward 0 stars. and are now free parameters with the same shapes as before, one row per member and one row per movie, each with columns. We write the minimizers as and , with rows and , to keep them apart from the SVD embeddings. The predicted rating is

and it is defined for every pair , including the missing ones. Those predictions are what we use to rank candidates.

There is no closed form for the minimizer, because the loss involves the product of two unknowns. The loss is not convex in jointly. But it becomes a ridge regression as soon as we fix one of the two matrices.

Alternating least squares (ALS) algorithm

Fix and look at the terms of the loss that involve a single member’s embedding . Let be the movies that member rated. The other members’ terms do not involve , so minimizing over means minimizing

This is a ridge regression of member ’s centered ratings on the embeddings of the movies they rated, with playing the role of the coefficients. Setting the gradient with respect to to zero,

Stack the rows for into the matrix , and the ratings into the vector of length . Then , and the update is

The inverse always exists: is positive semidefinite, and adding with makes it positive definite. By the symmetry of the loss, fixing and letting be the members who rated movie gives

ALS alternates between updating every and updating every . Each half-step minimizes the loss exactly over one matrix while the other is held fixed, so the loss can never increase. Because the joint problem is not convex, ALS converges to a local minimum that can depend on the starting point. The members’ updates do not depend on each other, and neither do the movies’, so each half-step parallelizes across machines.

Let’s fit the tiny Netflix ratings with ALS, using and .

Code 
observed <- !is.na(Y_star)
mu <- mean(Y_star[observed])
eta <- 1

# Ridge regression of each row of Y on the fixed embeddings, using only that row's observed entries
ridge_rows <- function(Y, fixed, observed) {
  map(seq_len(nrow(Y)), \(row) {
    O_row <- observed[row, ]                      # O_q for a member, O^j for a movie
    fixed_O <- fixed[O_row, , drop = FALSE]
    as.vector(solve(t(fixed_O) %*% fixed_O + eta * diag(d),
                    t(fixed_O) %*% (Y[row, O_row] - mu)))
  }) %>%
    list_c() %>%
    matrix(ncol = d, byrow = TRUE)
}

# One ALS iteration: update every phi_q with Psi fixed, then every psi_j with Phi fixed
als_step <- function(embeddings, iter) {
  Phi_star <- ridge_rows(Y_star, embeddings$Psi_star, observed)
  Psi_star <- ridge_rows(t(Y_star), Phi_star, t(observed))
  list(Phi_star = Phi_star, Psi_star = Psi_star)
}

loss <- function(embeddings) {
  e <- (Y_star - mu - embeddings$Phi_star %*% t(embeddings$Psi_star))[observed]
  sum(e^2) + eta * (sum(embeddings$Phi_star^2) + sum(embeddings$Psi_star^2))
}

set.seed(5)
embeddings_0 <- list(Phi_star = matrix(rnorm(nrow(Y_star) * d, sd = 0.1), ncol = d),
                     Psi_star = matrix(rnorm(ncol(Y_star) * d, sd = 0.1), ncol = d))
iterates <- accumulate(1:20, als_step, .init = embeddings_0)
losses <- map_dbl(iterates[-1], loss)
round(losses[c(1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20)], 3)
[1] 56.926 23.560 23.137 23.048 23.041 23.041

The loss falls at every iteration and levels off within a few. The predicted ratings fill in the whole matrix.

Code 
als_fit <- last(iterates)
Y_star_hat <- mu + als_fit$Phi_star %*% t(als_fit$Psi_star)
dimnames(Y_star_hat) <- dimnames(Y_star)
round(Y_star_hat, 1)
        Notebook Titanic LaLaLand DieHard Matrix Alien
member1      4.7     4.2      3.8     1.7    2.5   2.0
member2      4.2     5.1      4.3     2.2    1.6   1.7
member3      4.4     4.8      4.2     2.0    1.9   1.8
member4      1.5     1.8      2.3     4.7    4.1   4.5
member5      2.3     1.5      2.1     3.9    4.5   4.3
member6      2.0     1.4      2.1     4.2    4.5   4.5
member7      4.5     4.6      4.1     1.9    2.0   1.8

Every missing rating is predicted in line with the member’s taste. Member 1, who rated Notebook 5 stars and Die Hard 1 star, is predicted to give La La Land 3.8 stars and The Matrix 2.5. Member 5, an action fan, is predicted to give Die Hard 3.9 stars and Notebook 2.3. Nothing in the model restricts predictions to the 1 to 5 star scale, and member 2’s predicted rating for Titanic is 5.1.

The penalty matters a great deal here. There are 28 observed ratings and embedding parameters, so without a penalty the model could almost memorize the observed ratings and say little about the missing ones. With instead of 1, the same code predicts that member 2 would give Titanic 6.2 stars and Alien 0.7, both off the scale, and that member 5, an action fan, would give Notebook 3.9. In practice, and are chosen by holding out some observed ratings and measuring the error on them, which is exactly how the Netflix Prize scored entries.

Koren, Bell and Volinsky also replace the single average with a per-member and a per-movie baseline, to capture generous raters and popular movies. Nonnegative matrix factorization (Lee and Seung, 1999) is another variant: it constrains every entry of and to be nonnegative, so each latent taste can only add to an affinity, which often makes the dimensions easier to interpret. In every variant, the predicted affinity is still built on the dot product .

Cold start

Matrix factorization only knows about members and movies that appear in . A member who signed up today, or a Netflix original that premiered this morning, has no row or column and so no embedding. There are a few simple fixes.

Fold in new members without retraining. Because has orthonormal columns, is the first columns of the identity, so

Multiplying both sides on the right by and using ,

Each member’s embedding is a function of only their own row of and the fixed movie embeddings. So when a new member with engagement row (a vector) arrives, we compute

which is the sum of the embeddings of the movies they watched, with each dimension divided by its singular value. By symmetry, a new movie that a few existing members have watched gets , where is its column of engagement, with one entry per member. Two-tower embedding retrieval

The modern workhorse of candidate generation is the two-tower model, a direct descendant of matrix factorization. Matrix factorization is cheap at request time, and the reason is worth making explicit. The predicted affinity factorizes into a part that depends only on the member and a part that depends only on the movie. All the movie embeddings can be computed once, offline. When member opens the home page, we look up and score each candidate with a single dot product. The two-tower model keeps exactly this structure and changes only where the embeddings come from.

From lookup tables to neural networks. In matrix factorization, an embedding is a row of a table. If is a one-hot encoding of member ’s ID, a vector with a 1 in member ’s position and 0 elsewhere, then : a linear map applied to the member’s ID. Likewise , with the one-hot encoding of movie ’s ID. The two-tower model replaces each of these linear maps with a neural network, and replaces each one-hot ID with a richer description of the member or the title. The table lookups and become functions and , and the predicted affinity becomes a score,

As in the SVD, one side is about the member and the other is about the title. The query tower reads the member’s features: their recently watched titles, country, device and time of day. The title tower reads the title’s features: genre, cast, director, synopsis, maturity rating. Matrix factorization is the special case where the only feature is the ID and each tower is a single linear layer, and the content regression from the cold start section is a title tower with a single linear layer on content features.

The two towers have nothing in common but their output. Their inputs are different, not even of the same length, and the two networks typically share no parameters. The one requirement is that each tower ends in a layer with exactly outputs, so that the dot product

is defined. The member embedding and the title embedding are different objects that describe different things, exactly as row of describes a member and row of describes a movie in the SVD. What ties them together is that the dot product multiplies coordinate of one with coordinate of the other. For the score to be useful, coordinate must mean “how much the member likes latent taste ” on one side and “how much the title has latent taste ” on the other. In our tiny Netflix, Notebook’s movie embedding is and Die Hard’s is , so they sit on opposite sides of the romance versus action taste, and member 1’s affinity is 0.75 for Notebook and for Die Hard.

Nobody assigns these meanings in advance. They emerge because the two towers are trained jointly: the loss depends on the towers only through the dot products, so every gradient step updates both networks together, and each tower learns coordinates that line up with the other’s. The towers are separate networks, but they cannot be trained separately. What they can do is run separately once trained, which is where the savings come from:

  • The title embeddings do not depend on the member, so they are computed offline for all titles and refreshed as the catalog changes.
  • When the member opens the home page, we run once and search for the titles with the largest inner product.

The price of this separation is that cannot use cross features, features that describe the pair jointly, such as “this member finished season 1 of this show” or “this member has watched three other films by this director”. Such a feature belongs to neither tower alone. Cross features are left for phase 2.

The learned coordinates are also not unique. For any invertible matrix , replacing the embeddings with and leaves every score unchanged, since . The loss cannot tell the two sets of embeddings apart, so an individual coordinate has no fixed meaning unless something else pins it down. In the SVD, the orthonormal columns sorted by singular value pin the coordinates down up to sign, which is why our code had to flip signs to make the second taste read as romance. A two-tower network has no such constraint. This matters later: a cosine similarity between two title embeddings is unchanged when is orthogonal, but not for a general , so the similarity depends on choices made in training.

Advantages over matrix factorization. Replacing ID lookups with networks over features buys several things:

  • Cold start. Because reads content features, the Netflix original that premiered this morning gets an embedding on day one, with no views at all. Unlike the content regression we bolted onto matrix factorization, the title tower can be nonlinear and is trained jointly with the query tower, rather than fit afterward to embeddings learned without content.
  • Context. In matrix factorization, member has one embedding , whatever the context. The query tower can produce a different embedding for the same member on the living room TV on Friday night than on their phone during a weekday commute.
  • Freshness. Because reads the member’s recent viewing, their embedding changes the moment they finish a title, without refitting anything. This generalizes the fold-in formula , which is a fixed linear function of the viewing history, to a learned nonlinear one.
  • Sharing strength. Two titles with similar features get similar embeddings even if few members have watched both, so rarely watched titles borrow information from similar popular ones.

Training a two-tower model

To see what joint training means, make the parameters explicit. Write the query tower as , where collects all of its weights and biases, and the title tower as , where collects all of its weights and biases. The two sets are disjoint: no parameter belongs to both towers. The score is

In the matrix factorization special case, and : the parameters of each “tower” are just its embedding table.

The training data is a log of plays. Each element is a pair : the member’s state at the moment they pressed play, and the title they played. Following Covington, Adams and Sargin (2016), who introduced this framing for video recommendation, we treat retrieval as an extreme multiclass classification: given , which of the titles did the member play? A softmax over the catalog turns scores into probabilities,

and training minimizes the average negative log likelihood of the observed plays, jointly over both sets of parameters,

Substituting the softmax, the log of a ratio is the log of the numerator minus the log of the denominator, so each play contributes

Every term of involves both and , through the product of the two towers’ outputs.

Notice that contains only positives: it records the titles that were played, and has no records of titles that were not played. The negatives enter through the softmax denominator instead. The denominator sums over all titles in the catalog, not just the titles in , and after taking logs it becomes the log-sum-exp term above. So for every play , the numerator term rewards a high score for the played title , and the denominator term penalizes high scores for every title in the catalog. The net effect is to raise ’s score relative to all the others. Every title the member did not play acts as an implicit negative for that play. This carries the same caveat as missing ratings in matrix factorization: a title that was not played was not necessarily disliked. The member may simply never have seen it.

The gradients show why the towers cannot be trained separately. Take a single play and write its term of as . To shorten the notation, write for the member’s embedding, for title ’s embedding, and . The derivative of the log-sum-exp term with respect to is

so the gradients with respect to the two towers’ outputs are

The first is a vector built entirely from the title tower’s outputs. It pulls the member’s embedding toward the played title and away from the average title under the model’s current probabilities. The second is built entirely from the query tower’s output. It pulls the played title’s embedding toward the member, and pushes every other title away in proportion to its predicted probability. The chain rule carries these into the parameters,

where is the Jacobian of the query tower’s outputs with respect to its parameters, and is the Jacobian of the title tower for title . Backpropagation computes both. So the update to the query tower’s parameters requires the title tower’s current outputs, and the update to the title tower’s parameters requires the query tower’s current output. Each tower’s training signal comes from the other.

Let’s train a two-tower model on a small Netflix, with titles: 20 romances, 20 action movies and 20 family films, about half of them long. Title ’s features are , a genre indicator plus a runtime indicator. Each play comes from a member described by : the share of their history in each genre, and whether they are watching on the TV rather than a phone. We simulate 3,000 plays from a true model in which members play titles from their favorite genre, and prefer long titles on the TV and short ones on a phone.

Each tower has one hidden layer of 8 ReLU units and outputs,

so the query tower’s parameters are and the title tower’s are , with of size , , and of size .

In the code, X_q stacks the plays’ feature vectors as rows and F_titles stacks the titles’ , so the query tower’s output has row for each play and the title tower’s output has row for each title. The parameters are stored as a nested list omega, with one element per tower, omega$phi holding and omega$psi holding . With only 60 titles, we can afford the full sum over the catalog, and we run plain gradient descent on with learning rate alpha, which multiplies each gradient before it is subtracted from the parameters. Each step is a function gradient_step that takes the current parameters and returns updated ones, and accumulate applies it 1,000 times, keeping every intermediate set of parameters so that we can trace the loss. The matrix dS holds the derivative of with respect to each score, . Then dPhi and dPsi are exactly the two gradients above, averaged over plays, and the remaining lines carry them back through each tower’s layers.

set.seed(6)

N <- 60

long <- rbinom(N, 1, 0.5)
F_titles <- cbind(diag(3)[title_genre, ], long)            # row j is f_j

X_q <- cbind(share, on_tv)                                  # row q is x_q

# True model: favorite genre, long titles on the TV, short titles on a phone
true_score <- 4 * share[, title_genre] + 1.5 * outer(on_tv, long) + 1.5 * outer(1 - on_tv, 1 - long)
softmax_rows <- function(S) {
  row_max <- S[cbind(seq_len(nrow(S)), max.col(S, ties.method = "first"))]
  E <- exp(S - row_max)
  E / rowSums(E)
}
P_true <- softmax_rows(true_score)
j_played <- map_int(1:n_plays, \(q) sample(N, 1, prob = P_true[q, ]))
played <- cbind(1:n_plays, j_played)
J_true <- -mean(log(P_true[played]))                       # loss of the true model
Y_played <- matrix(0, n_plays, N)
Y_played[played] <- 1

# The two towers, each with one hidden layer of ReLU units
d <- 4
n_hidden <- 8
relu <- function(z) pmax(z, 0)
query_tower <- function(x, w) {
  Z <- sweep(x %*% w$G1, 2, w$g1, "+")
  list(Z = Z, A = relu(Z), out = relu(Z) %*% w$G2)
}
title_tower <- function(f, w) {
  Z <- sweep(f %*% w$H1, 2, w$h1, "+")
  list(Z = Z, A = relu(Z), out = relu(Z) %*% w$H2)
}

# Initialize the two towers' parameters separately
init <- function(r, c) matrix(rnorm(r * c, sd = 0.3), r, c)
omega_0 <- list(
  phi = list(G1 = init(ncol(X_q), n_hidden), g1 = rep(0, n_hidden), G2 = init(n_hidden, d)),
  psi = list(H1 = init(ncol(F_titles), n_hidden), h1 = rep(0, n_hidden), H2 = init(n_hidden, d))
)

two_tower_loss <- function(omega) {
  P <- softmax_rows(query_tower(X_q, omega$phi)$out %*% t(title_tower(F_titles, omega$psi)$out))
  -mean(log(P[played]))
}

alpha <- 0.5
gradient_step <- function(omega, iter) {
  # Forward pass through each tower, then the softmax over all N titles
  query_pass <- query_tower(X_q, omega$phi)
  title_pass <- title_tower(F_titles, omega$psi)
  P <- softmax_rows(query_pass$out %*% t(title_pass$out))

  # Gradients with respect to the scores and the two towers' outputs
  dS <- (P - Y_played) / n_plays
  dPhi <- dS %*% title_pass$out       # needs the title tower's outputs
  dPsi <- t(dS) %*% query_pass$out    # needs the query tower's outputs

  # Backpropagate through each tower to its own parameters
  dZ_q <- (dPhi %*% t(omega$phi$G2)) * (query_pass$Z > 0)
  dZ_t <- (dPsi %*% t(omega$psi$H2)) * (title_pass$Z > 0)
  gradient <- list(
    phi = list(G1 = t(X_q) %*% dZ_q, g1 = colSums(dZ_q), G2 = t(query_pass$A) %*% dPhi),
    psi = list(H1 = t(F_titles) %*% dZ_t, h1 = colSums(dZ_t), H2 = t(title_pass$A) %*% dPsi)
  )

  # Update both towers' parameters in the same step
  map2(omega, gradient, \(tower, d_tower) map2(tower, d_tower, \(w, dw) w - alpha * dw))
}

omega_trace <- accumulate(1:1000, gradient_step, .init = omega_0)
J_trace <- map_dbl(omega_trace, two_tower_loss)

)

Optimization using sampling

Although lists only plays, the loss and the gradients for each play contain a sum over all titles, which costs per play. That is wasteful when it is repeated over billions of plays. Instead, we estimate the sum by importance sampling. Draw negatives from a sampling distribution over titles, where is the probability of drawing title . Multiplying and dividing each term of the denominator by turns the sum into an expectation under , which the sample average estimates,

Each sampled term can be rewritten as

So sampled negatives enter the softmax with a corrected logit . The constant only shifts the loss, so it does not affect the gradient. The cheapest negatives are the titles that other members played in the same mini-batch (“in-batch negatives”). But those are drawn in proportion to how often titles are played, so is large for a hit like Stranger Things. Without the correction, Stranger Things appears as a negative in almost every batch, far more often than under uniform sampling, and the model learns to under-score it. Yi et al. (2019) apply this “logQ correction” to every logit in the batch softmax, estimate from streaming play counts, and serve with the uncorrected .

Phase 2: Predicting utility

Now we have a few hundred candidates instead of 10,000 titles, so we can afford a far more expensive model per title. The model receives a feature vector for each member and candidate pair. It includes member features (genre history, how much they watch on weeknights), title features (genre, runtime, popularity this week), context (TV or phone, Friday night), and the cross features that the two-tower model could not use (finished season 1 of this show). The model outputs , an estimate of .

What is utility?

Before choosing a model, we choose the outcome. Utility is the expected value of something we can measure for a displayed tile, . The choice of matters a lot:

  • Plays: indicates that the member pressed play, and is a play probability.
  • Minutes streamed: utility decomposes into whether the member plays the title and how long they watch once they do, each factor conditional on ,
  • Explicit feedback: whether the member gives the title a thumbs up.

What Netflix ultimately cares about is retention, whether the member keeps their subscription. Gomez-Uribe and Hunt report that viewing time is strongly correlated with retention, which is one reason engagement outcomes such as minutes streamed are useful proxies. Most systems care about several outcomes and combine them,

where is the -th outcome and the weights are a business choice, usually tuned with AB tests on retention and engagement.

Pointwise models

The simplest approach treats every displayed (member, title) tile as an independent row and fits a model to . For a play, that is logistic regression, , where , or a gradient boosted tree, or a neural network. A well-known design is Wide & Deep (Cheng et al., 2016). Its logit is the sum of a wide linear part on hand crafted cross features, which memorizes specific co-occurrences (“watched Breaking Bad” crossed with “candidate is Better Call Saul”), and a deep part, an MLP on learned embeddings, which generalizes to combinations it has never seen.
